column4: text

Each step down a group adds a whole new electron shell, so the outermost electrons sit farther from the nucleus. The extra protons are largely cancelled by the inner shells in between, which shield the outer electrons, so the pull those electrons feel barely grows while their distance does. The atom gets bigger at every step: in group 1, from lithium to caesium.

Across a period, each element adds one proton to the nucleus and one electron to the same outer shell. Electrons in the same shell shield each other poorly, so the effective nuclear charge on the outer electrons rises at every step and draws the whole shell in. Adding electrons does not make the atom bigger here: the stronger pull wins, and the radius shrinks from sodium to chlorine.

Ionization energy is the energy needed to remove an atom's outermost electron. Across a period the effective nuclear charge rises and the atom shrinks, so that electron is held more tightly and costs more to remove. It climbs from the alkali metal at the start of the period to the noble gas at its end, with two small dips along the way.

Down a group, the outermost electron sits in a shell farther from the nucleus each time, and the inner shells screen it from most of the added protons. Farther away and better shielded, it is easier to remove, so the first ionization energy falls step by step: in group 1 from lithium to caesium, which is why caesium gives up its electron so readily.

Two dips interrupt the rise across a period. Boron is lower than beryllium because its outer electron is the first in a 2p orbital, which is higher in energy and better shielded than 2s. Oxygen is lower than nitrogen because its fourth 2p electron has to share an orbital, and the repulsion between the paired electrons makes one of them easier to remove. The same two dips come again in period 3, at aluminium and sulfur.

Successive ionization energies rise as each electron is removed, because the ones that remain are held by the same nucleus with less repulsion between them. The big jump comes when the next electron has to come from a full inner shell, much closer to the nucleus and far less shielded. That is why sodium's second ionization energy is about ten times its first: the first empties the outer shell, the second breaks into the neon core.

Electronegativity is how strongly an atom pulls the shared electrons of a bond towards itself. Across a period the nuclear charge felt by the outer shell rises while the atom shrinks, so a bonding pair sits closer to a more strongly charged nucleus. The pull grows at each step, from sodium (0.93) to chlorine (3.16); the noble gases at the end rarely form bonds and usually have no value.

Down a group, the bonding electrons sit in a shell farther from the nucleus and are screened from it by more inner electrons. The nucleus pulls on them less, so electronegativity falls: fluorine is the most electronegative element of all, and each halogen below it pulls a little less.

Fluorine is the most electronegative element because its outer electrons are in the second shell, very close to a nucleus they are poorly shielded from, and it needs only one more electron to fill that shell. A bonding pair shared with fluorine is pulled towards it harder than towards any other atom: 3.98 on the Pauling scale, the highest of any element.

column4: The noble gases have a full outer shell: two electrons for helium, eight for the rest. A full shell is a particularly stable arrangement, so removing an electron costs a great deal of energy, and the noble gases have the highest ionization energies in their periods, while there is nothing to gain from taking one on. With nothing to gain from losing, gaining or sharing electrons, they form compounds only under extreme conditions, such as xenon with fluorine.

column4: The alkali metals have a single electron in their outer shell, and losing it leaves the stable arrangement of the noble gas before them. That electron is easy to remove, and easier the farther down the group it sits, because it is farther from the nucleus and better shielded. So reactivity rises down the group: lithium fizzes in water, sodium melts and darts across it, and potassium and the heavier metals ignite.

The halogens are one electron short of a full outer shell, and they react by gaining one. Fluorine's outer shell is closest to the nucleus and least shielded, so it attracts an incoming electron most strongly, which makes it the most reactive. Down the group the outer shell is farther away and better screened, the pull weakens, and the halogens become less reactive: chlorine, then bromine, then iodine.

Metallic character is how readily an element gives up electrons, which is what metals do. It follows ionization energy and electronegativity in reverse: the elements that hold their electrons most loosely are the most metallic. So it increases down a group and decreases across a period, which puts the most metallic elements at the bottom left of the table, the nonmetals at the top right, and the metalloids along the boundary between them.

Across period 3 the melting point rises to a peak at silicon and then collapses. Sodium, magnesium and aluminium are metals, held by a sea of electrons that grows stronger as each atom contributes more. Silicon is a giant covalent network, and melting it means breaking strong bonds throughout the solid. Phosphorus, sulfur and chlorine form small separate molecules held together only by weak forces, and argon is single atoms, so their melting points are low.

The alkali metals melt at lower temperatures down the group. Each atom gives a single electron to the metallic bond, and as the atoms grow larger that electron is spread over a bigger volume and held farther from the nuclei, so the bonding weakens. Lithium melts at 180.5 °C and caesium at 28.5 °C, warm enough to melt in a hand.

Density depends on how heavy the atoms are and how closely they pack. Atomic mass rises steadily through the table, but the atoms also shrink across each period, so the densest elements that have been measured are heavy transition metals in the middle of period 6, where a large mass sits in a small, tightly packed atom: osmium and iridium, at about 22.6 g/cm³. The gases at the top and the right are the least dense.

Across the lanthanides, electrons fill the 4f orbitals, which shield the outer electrons poorly. Each added proton therefore draws the outer shell in a little more, and the atoms shrink steadily from lanthanum to lutetium. The effect carries on beyond them: hafnium ends up almost exactly the size of zirconium above it, which is why the two are so hard to separate chemically.

Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature. Its outer 6s electrons are pulled unusually close to its heavy nucleus, a relativistic effect of the speed at which they move, so they are reluctant to take part in metallic bonding. With the bonds between its atoms weak, mercury melts at −38.8 °C, far below its neighbours gold and thallium.

In the liquid, the noble gases are held together only by London dispersion forces, which come from fleeting distortions of their electron clouds. Small atoms with few electrons distort least, so helium's forces are the weakest of any element and it boils at −268.9 °C, the lowest boiling point of all. Down the group the atoms grow larger and easier to distort, and the boiling points rise.

Electron affinity is the energy released when an atom gains an electron. Across a period the incoming electron is drawn by a growing effective nuclear charge into a shrinking atom, so more energy is released, and the halogens release the most because one electron completes their outer shell. The rise is uneven: magnesium releases almost none because the new electron must start the 3p subshell, phosphorus little because it must pair up in a half-filled one, and argon none because it must start a new shell.
